items.headline: Need a tea-time snack idea? Try this delicious beetroot and feta cheese kachori
items.body: Try this beetroot and feta cheese kachori next time you are hosting friends Chef shares beetroot and feta cheese kachori recipe. Kachoris are deep-fried snacks with spicy fillings. Serve kachoris with mint or saunth chutneys for extra flavor. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Kachoris are flavourful snacks that make for wonderful accompaniments to tea, whether it's mid-morning or evening. They are a classic street treat known for its flaky exterior and soft, spicy filling. While there are many variations of the delicacy, the standard form is round, deep-fried pastry made from all-purpose flour (maida) and stuffed with a variety of fillings. These kachoris are often served with delicious chutneys that make every bite even more enjoyable. Dominic Gerard, Executive Chef of the 080 Lounge operated by TFS at T1, BLR Airport, shared with Moneycontrol a recipe for beetroot and feta cheese kachori, which you’d love to try and enjoy with your family and friends. Recipe for Beetroot and Feta Cheese Kachori Also read | Tired of the same old meals? Use these easy recipes to transform everyday ingredients into delights Ingredients (for 20 Kachoris) For the filling: Beetroot: 300 gm Feta cheese: 100 gm Chopped chilli: 20 gm Chopped ginger: 10 gm Chopped coriander leaves: 15 gm Asafoetida powder: 2 gm Cumin powder: 5 gm Chaat masala: 10 gm Salt: To Taste Oil refined: 25 ml Fennel seeds: 3 gm Crushed coriander seed: 3 gm Kachori dough Maida: 500 gm Ghee and Oil: 150 gm Rava/Semolina: 50 gm Salt: 10 gm Water: 120 ml Preparation: Stuffing Peel and grate the beetroot, squeeze out excess moisture and set aside. In a heavy-bottomed pan, heat oil and add the chopped green chilli and ginger. Allow them to sweat, then sprinkle the asafoetida and stir well. Add the grated beet and sauté till evenly coated and the moisture evaporates. Also read | 11 easy recipes to get most out of the health benefits of peaches Add the powdered spices along with the crushed coriander seeds and fennel, and cook until the beetroot softens. Season with salt and chaat masala, being careful to keep it moderate, as the feta will also add to the seasoning. Remove from heat and set aside to cool down. Once cold, add the crumbled feta and gently mix in. Kachori dough Sift the refined flour and semolina into a mixing bowl. Add salt, oil and ghee and rub it through to resemble breadcrumbs. Carefully add water and mix it into a dough without much kneading. The dough needs to be firm, neither too soft nor too hard. Rest the prepared dough for about 30 minutes covered with a damp cheesecloth. Divide the prepared dough into 20 balls of 40 g each. Flatten the dough between the palm or using a rolling pin to about 3-inch diameter. Spoon out about 30 g of the prepared beetroot and feta filling in the centre. Carefully cover from the sides and reshape it into a ball with the filling in the centre, and seal it well. Complete for all the 20 kachoris. Meanwhile, heat oil in a kadhai or wok to moderate heat. Press each of the prepared balls between the palm and add it to the moderately heated oil. Slowly fry them for a good 10-12 minutes on moderate heat. Transfer the kachoris with a slotted spoon onto a plate lined with an absorbent kitchen napkin to drain off excess oil. Serve alone or with mint and saunth chutneys.
items.snippet: If you love a savoury delight with your tea, try this beetroot and feta cheese kachori. With its flavourful filling and flaky outer shell, it’s going to be loved by your family and friends.

items.headline: Vodafone Idea share price: Citi removes ‘High Risk’ rating, sees up to 22% upside potential; here’s why
items.body: After a steep selloff last year, Vodafone Idea shares have nearly doubled over the past 12 months, helped by AGR relief hopes and improving investor sentiment. Citi has now removed its 'High Risk' rating on the stock and raised its target price to Rs 17, implying an upside potential of about 22% from the previous closing price.In its latest note, Citi Research changed its rating on Vodafone Idea shares to ‘Buy’ from ‘Buy-High Risk’, taking several tailwinds including the government’s recent reassessment of AGR dues, rating upgrades, equity infusion by the Aditya Birla Group, and other factors into consideration.“The company's balance sheet leverage has been uncomfortably high and worsened following the adverse Supreme Court verdict on the AGR issue in October 2019. However, government moves since then, including a moratorium on spectrum and AGR payments, partial conversion of spectrum dues to equity, and reassessment of AGR dues have together provided material balance sheet and cash flow relief. Planned equity infusion by the AB Group is an additional positive, which should enable the company to complete its long-pending bank fund raise, thereby resuming network investments,” it said.Investor sentiment got a boost in May after the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) cut Vodafone Idea's AGR dues by 27% to Rs 64,046 crore as of December 31. The stock received another lift when the company reappointed Kumar Mangalam Birla as non-executive chairman, nearly five years after he stepped down amid the telco's financial troubles.Citi said Vodafone Idea has laid out an aggressive three-year growth plan involving Rs 45,000 crore of capex. The investment will focus on expanding 4G and 5G coverage across its 17 priority circles, upgrading all 2G sites to 4G in five non-priority circles, and rolling out fixed wireless access (FWA) services.The brokerage, however, flagged key risks to its bullish view, including delays in bank funding, intensifying competition that could limit future tariff hikes, continued subscriber churn, and slower-than-expected growth in 4G and 5G users.Vodafone Idea share priceVodafone Idea shares were trading marginally higher at around Rs 14 apiece on Tuesday. The stock has slipped over 1% in the past week but gained more than 36% in the last month and nearly doubled over the past year.The stock has jumped 95% in three years and 58% in five years. The company currently has a market capitalisation of more than Rs 1.52 lakh crore.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
items.snippet: Vodafone Idea shares have seen significant gains. Citi has upgraded its rating to 'Buy' and set a new target price. This positive outlook is driven by government relief on AGR dues and improved investor confidence. The company is also planning substantial network investments to boost its 4G and 5G services.

items.headline: How to create a cosy corner at home: Easy ideas for everyday comfort
items.body: Bring in a bit of nature with plants. Even one or two small plants can make the space feel fresh and lively. They add colour and a sense of peace to your corner (Image: Pexels) Create a cosy corner with soft seating and colourful cushions Use a jute rug and soft lighting for warmth and comfort Add plants and personal items to make the space inviting Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Having a personal corner in your home is one of life’s small comforts. It is a place where you can slow down, read a book, sip tea, or simply sit quietly. In a busy home, this little space becomes your own. The good news is, you don’t need much to create it. You don’t always need an elaborate plan or expensive furniture to create a cosy corner. Here are some simple tips Start with any small space , a corner of your room, a spot near a window, or even a little unused area in the living room. The idea is to keep things simple and comfortable. Also read | 5 smart décor tips to revamp your rental home Add seating that feels relaxed. It could be a soft chair, a bean bag, or even a floor mattress. Layer it with colourful cushions to bring life to the space. Cushions not only add comfort but also make the corner look warm and inviting. A jute rug can change the whole feel of your corner. It adds texture and gives a natural, earthy touch. Place it under your seating to define the space. It makes the corner feel complete and cosy. Lighting is very important. Avoid bright, harsh lights. Instead, use a soft lamp that gives a warm glow. A small table lamp or floor lamp works perfectly. It creates a calm mood, especially in the evening. Also read | Home decor tips: How handcrafted elements are bringing warmth back into urban homes Bring in a bit of nature with plants. Even one or two small plants can make the space feel fresh and lively. They add colour and a sense of peace to your corner. Make the space personal. Keep a few books nearby, on a small table or a simple ladder shelf. Add wall art or wallpaper behind your corner to give it character. It could be something colourful, something that makes you feel happy. A cosy corner does not need to be perfect. It just needs to feel right to you. With simple things like cushions, a rug, a lamp, and a few personal touches, you can create a space where you truly enjoy spending time.
items.snippet: Home decor tips: A cosy corner is a small, personal space where you can relax and unwind. You don’t need expensive furniture or a big area, simple touches like colourful cushions, soft lighting, plants, and books can turn any corner into a warm and inviting retreat.

items.headline: Vodafone Idea to tweak tariffs selectively, no immediate plan for price hike: CEO
items.body: After several years of subscriber decline, Vodafone Idea has started to show early signs of recovery, with improved additions in February and March Vodafone Idea plans selective tariff adjustments, not broad hikes Airtel hikes 84-day prepaid plan price from ₹859 to ₹899 Vodafone Idea added over 1 lakh subscribers in March Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Telecom operator Vodafone Idea is looking at selective adjustments to its existing mobile tariffs, with no immediate plans for an across-the-board rate hike. The remarks come soon after Bharti Airtel, India’s second-largest telecom operator by market share, raised the price of one of its long-validity prepaid plans— a move analysts see as a potential test case for broader tariff hikes. “Minor corrections will be there but not a structural hike as you generally see,” Vodafone Idea Chief Executive Officer Abhijit Kishore told reporters. He added that continued government backing as a key shareholder remains encouraging, even as the company focuses on improving operational performance. After several years of subscriber decline, Vodafone Idea has started to show early signs of recovery, with improved additions in February and March. The company added over 1 lakh mobile subscribers in March, according to the latest Trai report. Related Stories Vodafone Idea begins next phase of 5G rollout across 23 cities Vodafone Idea aims to consolidate 4G coverage expansion in Bengal before 5G rollout: Official Nokia to have 3,300 sites ready by March to expand Vodafone Idea’s 4G network Bharti Airtel on Sunday raised the price of its Re 859 prepaid plan—offering 84 days validity with 1.5 GB of data per day—to Re 899, while discontinuing its Re 799 plan with 77-day validity, according to its website. The move is significant as headline tariffs across plans have remained largely unchanged for nearly two years. While such increases may weigh on consumers, operators argue they are essential to improve returns and recover heavy investments in 5G infrastructure. Analysts said Airtel’s Re 40 increase on the popular plan—about a 4.7 per cent hike—is likely to deliver only a modest uplift in average revenue per user (ARPU), a key metric that tracks monthly revenue per subscriber. However, some experts see the move as a calibrated market test, allowing Airtel to gauge the response of high-value users and potentially paving the way for gradual, more meaningful tariff increases. Airtel currently leads the industry in ARPU at Re 259, followed by Reliance Jio at Re 213.7 and Vodafone Idea at Re 172.

items.headline: Eternal to Minda Corp: Axis Securities picks 15 stocks for June, sees up to 44% upside in top ideas
items.body: Axis Securities has retained a constructive stance on Indian equities despite rising geopolitical risks and elevated crude oil prices, recommending 15 stock picks for June across largecap, midcap and smallcap segments with potential upside of up to 44%.In its latest monthly strategy report, the brokerage said domestic macroeconomic fundamentals remain resilient even as global uncertainties linked to the West Asia conflict, higher crude prices, rupee weakness and foreign investor outflows continue to weigh on market sentiment.The brokerage maintained its December 2026 Nifty target at 27,220 and said market corrections should be used selectively to accumulate quality businesses with strong earnings visibility.Axis Securities refreshed its list of 15 top stock picks, booking profits in SBI and exiting Max Healthcare while adding Varun Beverages and ICICI Bank.The brokerage's June list comprises nine largecap stocks, one midcap stock and five smallcap names. Among largecaps, Axis Securities recommended Eternal with the highest upside potential of 44%, followed by Bharti Airtel with 38% upside and ICICI Bank with 35% upside.Other large-cap recommendations include Bajaj Finance Limited, Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited, Avenue Supermarts, Varun Beverages, LG Electronics India and Nestle India. In the mid-cap space, the brokerage selected Dalmia Bharat with a target price implying nearly 39% upside from current levels.Among smallcap recommendations, Ujjivan Small Finance Bank emerged as the most preferred idea with a projected upside of 43%. Other smallcap picks include Chalet Hotels, Minda Corporation, Navin Fluorine and Kalpataru Projects.The brokerage said it continues to favour sectors where earnings visibility remains strong despite macroeconomic challenges.It remains overweight on banking and financial services, telecom, capital goods, healthcare, power and energy. It also maintains a positive view on selected consumption and retail businesses and continues to prefer certain capex-linked cyclical companies where valuations have become more attractive after the recent correction.On the other hand, the brokerage remains cautious on the information technology sector due to uncertainties arising from artificial intelligence-driven disruption and concerns around global technology spending. It noted that the Indian market has undergone a meaningful valuation reset over the past several months.According to the report, Indian equities are now trading at around 18 times one-year forward earnings, closer to long-term averages. The premium of Indian equities over emerging markets has also moderated sharply from nearly 97% in September 2024 to about 46% currently.Axis Securities said the recent correction has improved the medium-term attractiveness of Indian equities, although further upside will increasingly depend on corporate earnings delivery and companies' ability to manage higher input costs, logistics expenses and inflationary pressures.The brokerage expects India's GDP growth to remain in the 6.8%-6.9% range in FY27, supported by strong domestic demand, government capital expenditure and a gradual recovery in private investment.However, it warned that sustained crude oil prices, currency depreciation, rising inflation and weak monsoon conditions linked to El Niño remain key risks for both economic growth and market valuations.Also read: PSU bank stocks vs private banks in FY27: The valuation trap you need to avoidDespite these concerns, the brokerage said India continues to offer one of the strongest structural growth stories among major economies and expects Nifty earnings to grow at a 13% compound annual growth rate over FY23-28.For investors, Axis Securities recommended maintaining 10-15% liquidity to deploy during market corrections while focusing on high-quality companies with strong balance sheets and earnings visibility over the next 12-18 months.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. These do not represent the views of Economic Times)
items.snippet: Axis Securities retained a bullish view on Indian equities and recommended 15 stocks for June across market capitalisations, with potential upside of up to 44%. The brokerage favours banking, telecom and capital goods sectors, while remaining cautious on IT. It expects market corrections to offer opportunities to accumulate quality businesses.

items.headline: Vodafone Idea expects AGR reassessment outcome soon: CEO Abhijit Kishore
items.body: Vodafone Idea Vodafone Idea Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Abhijit Kishore on Friday said the long-awaited reassessment of adjusted gross revenue (AGR) dues is currently underway, with the company expecting clarity from the government-appointed Department of Telecommunications (DoT) committee soon. “The reassessment is ongoing. We are just waiting… hopefully it should happen as soon as possible,” Kishore said, adding that while there have been informal indications on timelines, the company is awaiting formal communication from the government. He declined to confirm any specific deadline, even as market expectations point to a possible June outcome. The DoT had set up a committee to re-examine—an issue that has weighed heavily on the telecom sector, particularly Vodafone Idea, which continues to grapple with substantial statutory dues. Operational recovery begins to show Even as regulatory clarity remains pending, Kishore pointed to early signs of improvement in operations. Citing data released by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI), he said the company has moved from negative to positive subscriber additions in recent months. Related Stories Vodafone Idea Q1 net loss narrows to Rs 3,754 crore; revenue up 6% Indus Towers, Vodafone Idea gain up to 2.6% after Nomura's telecom outlook Vodafone Idea shares jump 6.5% in 4-day rally, stock up nearly 45% in one month “You can see a clear improvement… we’ve moved from negative customer addition into a positive trajectory,” he said, signalling stabilisation in Vodafone Idea’s core mobility business. On reports of potential infrastructure-sharing arrangements and collaborations in emerging areas such as AI-led network security, Kishore remained non-committal. “There’s a lot of work happening… we’ll come back at the right time,” he said, without elaborating on possible partnerships. He also declined to comment on the financial implications of the reassessment, including figures circulating in the public domain, reiterating that the company will wait for the government’s final position. AI focus, but no clear roadmap yet Kishore acknowledged growing industry attention on advanced AI systems, including those being developed by Anthropic, particularly around their ability to detect vulnerabilities and potential data security risks. Without confirming any specific tie-ups, he said Vodafone Idea is actively working to strengthen network resilience and security frameworks, reflecting broader industry efforts to explore next-generation AI capabilities. However, he cautioned that it is still too early to outline deployment timelines or determine whether such technologies would require regulatory backing. The DoT recently extended the deadline for reassessing Vodafone Idea’s AGR dues by three months to June 30, as field units continue to face challenges in completing the exercise, according to sources. The extension follows the Supreme Court of India allowing the Centre to recalculate the telco’s AGR liabilities for the FY07–FY19 period. Subsequently, the Union Cabinet in January cleared the reassessment process, directing the DoT’s Controller of Communication Accounts (CCAs) to review licence fee and spectrum usage charge payments within a defined timeline. While the reassessment of licence fees has been completed, the recalculation of spectrum usage charges remains ongoing. Officials cited operational hurdles, including gaps in documentation. In several telecom circles, Vodafone Idea has struggled to provide legacy records required for validation, slowing the process. Given these bottlenecks, the extended timeline is expected to give field units additional time to complete the exercise and submit their findings.

items.headline: Quote of the day by Swami Vivekananda: “Take up one idea. Make that one idea your life; dream of it; think of it; live…”
items.body: Quote of the day by Swami Vivekananda: “Take up one idea. Make that one idea your life; dream of it; think of it; live on that idea..." Swami Vivekananda's quote stresses strong focus on one goal Success needs patience, commitment, and focused attention Consistency and belief in your idea are key to meaningful success Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Everyone wants to achieve success, many opt for short cuts. But that isn’t the right way. True success needs patience, focus, and deep commitment. Swami Vivekananda, the great Indian monk and thinker who inspired millions through his teachings on discipline, focus, and inner strength, once said: “Take up one idea. Make that one idea your life; dream of it; think of it; live on that idea. Let the brain, the body, muscles, nerves, every part of your body be full of that idea, and just leave every other idea alone. This is the way to success, and this is the way great spiritual giants are produced.” What does the quote mean? The quote is about focus in life. It tells us to choose one clear goal and give it our full attention. Instead of running after many things at once, we should stay loyal to one idea. When we think about it daily, work on it, and shape our life around it, it becomes stronger. Also read | Quote of the day by APJ Abdul Kalam: “We should not give up and we should…” It also means we must avoid distractions . In today’s world, people often change goals quickly. They get bored or compare themselves with others. But this quote reminds us that success comes from staying steady. When every part of your mind and body is working towards one aim, your efforts become powerful. You stop wasting energy on unimportant things. Slowly, your idea grows, and so do you. Remember, it is about giving your best to one purpose and trusting the process. How is it relevant today? People are easily distracted by social media and trends Many try to do too many things at once and lose focus Quick success is often preferred over meaningful success Career confusion is very common among young people Deep work and patience are becoming rare but valuable Consistency is needed more than ever in a fast-moving world Also read | Quote of the day by Homi J Bhabha: "No power is as costly as no power...." Lessons from the quote Focus on one goal at a time Avoid unnecessary distractions Be patient with your journey Give your full effort to your work Believe in your idea even when it is hard Success is built slowly, not instantly Tips to follow the quote Choose one clear goal and write it down Set a daily routine around your goal Limit time spent on distractions like social media Remind yourself daily why you started Break your goal into small, simple steps Stay consistent even when you feel tired Surround yourself with people who support your focus
items.snippet: This quote by Swami Vivekananda teaches that success is not about doing many things, but about doing one thing with full heart and full effort. Here’s how.

items.headline: ‘Make everyone drive ambulance first’: Pune cab driver’s late night idea about traffic jam solution in Ind
items.body: Some conversations start as small talk and end up changing the way you think about everyday life. A 4 am Uber ride in Pune became exactly that kind of moment for a US-based founder. What began as a quiet, half-asleep drive through empty roads soon turned into an unexpected discussion on India’s traffic chaos. But it wasn’t a complaint or a rant. It was a solution proposed by an Uber driver with years of experience behind the wheel of an ambulance, and it left the founder completely stunned.US-based founder recently shared his experience of being in Pune and taking an Uber ride early in the morning. He described the scene as quiet and almost surreal. The roads were empty, the city still half asleep, and the ride felt like one of those slow moments where random conversations naturally begin just to stay awake.According to him, the driver suddenly brought up India’s traffic problem and said it had a “very simple solution.” At first, the founder admitted he almost laughed it off. He mentioned that many people casually offer opinions on traffic, and it often feels like the same recycled ideas. But then the driver revealed something unexpected.He said he had driven an ambulance for 11 years. That changed the tone of the conversation instantly.From casual chatter, the ride shifted into something far more serious. The driver then shared his idea. He suggested that before giving anyone a driving license, people should be made to drive an ambulance for one week. Not sit inside one. Actually drive it. He explained what that would really mean. The siren is constantly screaming. A patient struggling to breathe in the back. Family members panicking beside them. Every traffic signal feels like a countdown to something critical.In that scenario, traffic is no longer an inconvenience. It becomes something far more urgent. He also described what he had witnessed during his 11 years of ambulance driving. He spoke about people refusing to give way even when an ambulance was behind them. Cars blocking junctions without hesitation. Vehicles stopping “just for 2 minutes” in the worst possible spots. And even situations where drivers tried to overtake an ambulance just to save a few seconds.131402734According to the founder’s account, these experiences shaped the driver's view of everyday road behaviour. Then came the line that shifted the entire mood of the ride. He said, “When you drive your own car, traffic is an inconvenience. When you drive an ambulance, traffic is life or death.” That one sentence left the Uber ride in silence.The founder described it as one of those moments where a simple idea suddenly feels heavier than expected. It reframes something ordinary into something deeply emotional. The driver’s perspective was not about blaming people or calling out bad habits in an aggressive way. Instead, it came from years of seeing how small decisions on the road can have serious consequences when time is critical.131403471He suggested that a week of driving an ambulance could teach more about discipline and road awareness than a standard driving test ever does. The idea stayed with the founder long after the ride ended. As he reflected on it, he admitted that it did not even sound like a bad idea anymore. The thought of making new drivers experience urgency from the perspective of emergency response made him reconsider how people learn road responsibility in the first place.What made the experience even more striking was its simplicity. There were no statistics or formal arguments, just one lived experience shared in the middle of a sleepy Uber ride at 4 am in Pune. The founder summed it up by saying that one of the smartest things he heard that month came from a sleep-deprived conversation with a driver on an otherwise empty road.131382507Internet reactsInternet users reacted strongly to the Pune Uber story, sharing varied perspectives on the idea. One user suggested that every individual should be made to serve in the Defence services for at least three years before starting their careers, saying it could transform society.Another user called it a “powerful yet humbling take,” adding that such conversations remind people to keep travelling and learning from real experiences, even comparing it to a story where survival changes outcomes more than strength. One comment highlighted how traffic is usually seen as an inconvenience, but rarely as someone else’s emergency, calling the shift in perspective deeply meaningful.
items.snippet: An Uber driver in Pune, with 11 years of ambulance experience, shared a profound idea with a US founder: make new drivers operate an ambulance for a week before getting a license. This experience, he argued, would instill a life-or-death urgency, fostering greater road discipline and awareness than any standard test.

items.headline: Quote of the day by Victor Hugo: "No army can withstand the strength of an idea whose..."
items.body: Quote of the day by Victor Hugo: "No army can withstand the strength of an idea whose..." (image: wikimedia) Victor Hugo's quote highlights the unstoppable power of ideas His works like Les Misérables shaped global views on justice Hugo's legacy inspires ongoing discussions on human rights Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Quote of the Day by Victor Hugo: The quote of the day by Victor Hugo, “No army can withstand the strength of an idea whose time has come,” continues to inspire readers across the world. This powerful line reflects the enduring influence of ideas, social change, and human resilience. As one of the most celebrated figures in world literature, Victor Hugo’s words remain deeply relevant in modern discussions on justice, freedom, and progress. Meaning of Victor Hugo’s quote Victor Hugo’s quote highlights the unstoppable nature of powerful ideas. It suggests that when the right moment arrives, no force can suppress truth, reform, or collective will. The message connects strongly with themes of social justice, human rights, and political change, showing how ideas can shape history and society. The quote also encourages individuals to believe in the power of thought and action. It reminds readers that meaningful change often begins with a simple idea that grows over time. Who was Victor Hugo Victor Hugo was a French poet, novelist, and playwright who became a leading voice of the Romantic movement. Born in 1802, he lived through major political changes in France and used his writing to address issues like poverty, injustice, and inequality. He was not only a literary figure but also a strong advocate for democratic rights and human dignity. His life reflected courage, especially during times of political unrest and exile. Victor Hugo’s most famous works Victor Hugo created some of the most influential works in world literature. His writing continues to be widely read and studied. Les Misérables explored themes of justice, redemption, and social inequality Notre Dame de Paris highlighted history, architecture, and human struggle Les Châtiments expressed strong opposition to political oppression These works helped shape global conversations about morality and society. Political life and exile Victor Hugo played an active role in politics and openly criticized injustice. He supported universal suffrage, education for all, and the abolition of the death penalty. When political conditions worsened under Napoleon III, Hugo chose exile rather than silence. During his years away from France, he continued to write and raise his voice against oppression. His exile strengthened his image as a symbol of resistance and integrity. Why Victor Hugo’s quote still matters In today’s world, the quote of the day by Victor Hugo holds strong relevance. From social movements to global debates on equality, the idea that change cannot be stopped once it gains momentum remains powerful. The quote reminds readers that ideas are stronger than force. It encourages patience, belief, and commitment to truth. Whether in personal growth or societal change, the message continues to guide people toward progress. Victor Hugo’s legacy and influence Victor Hugo’s influence extends beyond literature. His thoughts inspired writers, leaders, and reformers across generations. Even today, his works are adapted into films, plays, and discussions around human rights. His legacy proves that words can shape societies and ideas can outlast power. Through his life and writing, Hugo showed that courage and creativity can work together to create lasting impact. The quote of the day by Victor Hugo is more than a statement. It is a reminder that ideas have the power to transform the world. His life and work continue to inspire those who believe in justice, truth, and the strength of human thought.
items.snippet: Victor Hugo’s famous quote highlights the unstoppable power of ideas. Explore its meaning, his life, and why his words on justice and change still inspire today.

items.headline: Quote of the day by Mary Kay Ash: ‘A mediocre idea that generates enthusiasm will go further than a great…
items.body: Quote of the day: Some entrepreneurs build companies. Others build movements that change the lives of millions. Mary Kay Ash belonged firmly in the second category. Long before conversations about women breaking glass ceilings became mainstream, the cosmetics mogul was encouraging women to believe in their talents, financial independence and personal worth. Her rise from a young Texas girl caring for her ill father to the founder of a global beauty empire became one of America’s most inspiring business stories.Known for her motivational spirit, pink Cadillacs and people-first philosophy, Ash believed success was less about flawless ideas and more about inspiring others to believe in them wholeheartedly.Quote of the day today“A mediocre idea that generates enthusiasm will go further than a great idea that inspires no one.”The quote perfectly captures the philosophy that helped Mary Kay Ash transform a modest startup into one of the world’s most recognized beauty brands. While many leaders focus only on strategy or innovation, Ash believed passion, encouragement and human connection were often the true engines behind success.131373381Her words continue to resonate with entrepreneurs, creators, managers and dreamers navigating a world where enthusiasm can make the difference between an idea that fades away and one that changes lives.Who was Mary Kay Ash?Born Mary Kathlyn Wagner on May 12, 1918, in Hot Wells, Texas, Ash grew up during difficult economic times. Her mother worked long hours managing a café while her father struggled with illness, leaving young Mary Kay with major responsibilities at home from an early age.Those early experiences shaped the confidence and work ethic that later defined her career. Even as a child, she showed remarkable communication and sales abilities, convincing store clerks to let her shop independently and excelling in school competitions, debates and fundraising activities.After marrying young and raising three children, Ash entered the world of direct sales at a time when opportunities for women were severely limited. She worked for companies including Stanley Home Products and World Gift Company, where she consistently outperformed colleagues but repeatedly faced gender discrimination.In one especially painful moment, a man she had trained was promoted above her and given a much higher salary. Instead of giving up, Ash used her frustrations as motivation to create a business where women would be valued, rewarded and encouraged to succeed.That dream became reality in 1963 when she launched Mary Kay Cosmetics with just $5,000 in savings.Quote of the day meaningMary Kay Ash’s quote highlights a truth many people overlook: excitement and belief often matter more than perfection. A brilliant idea can fail if nobody feels emotionally connected to it. Meanwhile, an ordinary concept backed by passion, energy and confidence can inspire teams, customers and communities to rally behind it.131372186Ash understood this deeply because her business was built on motivation. She didn’t just sell beauty products — she sold encouragement, recognition and possibility. Her famous pink Cadillacs and lavish sales conventions were not random gimmicks. They were carefully designed symbols of enthusiasm and achievement.The quote also applies beyond business.A teacher who genuinely inspires students may leave a bigger impact than one with perfect credentials.A creative project fueled by excitement often gains more attention than technically flawless work lacking emotion.A workplace with motivated employees frequently outperforms one filled with talented but disconnected workers.In essence, Ash believed people are moved by energy and belief as much as by ideas themselves.Building a company around encouragementMary Kay Cosmetics became famous not only for makeup products but also for its culture of recognition. Ash believed praise was one of the most powerful tools a leader could use.She personally wrote notes, made phone calls and applauded achievements publicly. Consultants who excelled were rewarded with jewelry, vacations, fur coats and eventually the iconic pink Cadillacs that became synonymous with the brand.At a time when many corporations were dominated by rigid hierarchies and male leadership, Ash created a system where women could set their own schedules, build businesses independently and advance without traditional barriers.By the early 1990s, the company operated internationally and was recognized as one of the best places to work in America. Ash herself became one of the most celebrated female entrepreneurs of the 20th century.Why her message still resonates todayIn today’s world of startups, social media and constant competition, Mary Kay Ash’s quote feels more relevant than ever.People are often told they need the perfect business plan, flawless timing or groundbreaking innovation before starting something new. Ash’s words push back against that fear-driven mindset. Her philosophy suggests that belief, energy and emotional connection can carry people further than perfection ever could.That message especially resonates in creative industries and entrepreneurship, where confidence and momentum often determine whether an idea survives long enough to grow.131355629Ash also understood something deeply human: people want to feel seen, valued and inspired. Her success came not only from selling cosmetics but from building confidence in others.A legacy larger than beauty productsMary Kay Ash died in 2001, but her influence continues to extend far beyond the beauty industry. She remains a symbol of resilience, leadership and empowerment for women around the world.Her company created opportunities for countless people seeking financial independence and flexible careers. More importantly, her philosophy encouraged individuals to believe their enthusiasm, persistence and self-confidence mattered.The quote reflects that success is rarely powered by ideas alone. Often, it is belief, contagious, emotional and deeply human that turns an ordinary vision into something unforgettable.
items.snippet: Quote of the day: Mary Kay Ash died in 2001, but her influence continues to reach far beyond the beauty industry. She remains a lasting symbol of resilience, leadership and female empowerment around the world. Her company created opportunities for countless individuals seeking financial independence, entrepreneurial freedom and more flexible career paths.

items.headline: RSS 'hates' Dravidian idea, wants to rule TN: Rahul Gandhi at Kanniyakumari
items.body: The Tamil people have their own history of thousands of years, and they have their language, says Congress leader Rahul Gandhi At a rally in Kanyakumari, Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi on Monday attacked the BJP alleging that it is attempting to gain a foothold in Tamil Nadu through the AIADMK He also accused the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) of opposing the Dravidian ideology and seeking to assert control over the state. "I walked on the 'Bharat Jodo Yatra' from Kanyakumari to Kashmir. The idea of the yatra was to unite the country, which is why it was called Bharat Jodo Yatra. It aimed to send the message that India is made up of different ideas, languages, traditions, histories, and religions, and all of them must stand together in harmony, love, and affection. That is why the yatra was important. In this country, there are different religions, languages, histories, traditions, and cultures. But we have to unite all these people and make them live as one. That was the main purpose of the yatra. We are fighting an ideological battle with the BJP and the RSS, who believe in a fundamentally different concept of India..." he said. According to Gandhi, people of each state should run their state. "But the BJP does not think like this. it believes is one tradition, one language and one history," the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha said. #WATCH | Kanniyakumari, Tamil Nadu: Lok Sabha LoP and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi says, "A few days ago in parliament, the Prime Minister did a very dangerous thing. He told the country that he wanted to pass a women's bill, but the real plan was to change the electoral structure of… pic.twitter.com/M8JoKeBgaf — ANI (@ANI) April 20, 2026 Underscoring federal principles, Gandhi said every state should have its own voice and representation. "People of each state should run their state. But the BJP does not think like this. it believes is one tradition, one language and one history," the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha said. Gandhi said Tamil Nadu should be governed by its people. The Congress leader further alleged that US President Donald Trump sought to influence Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who inturn wanted to control TN through AIADMK chief Edappadi K Palaniswami. "The DMK and Congress were committed to protecting the Tamil Language, culture and its history," he said.
items.snippet: We are fighting an ideological battle with the BJP and the RSS, who believe in a fundamentally different concept of India, says Gandhi ahead of Tamil Nadu election

items.headline: Quote of the Day by Nobel Prize-winning German novelist Günter Grass: ‘No idea stays pure, even the flower
items.body: Quote of the Day: Günter Grass was a German novelist, poet, playwright, sculptor, printmaker, and artist whose influential works shaped post‑war literature. Born October 16, 1927, in Danzig (now Gdańsk, Poland), Günter Grass lived through the turbulence of World War II and became the literary spokesman for the German generation that grew up in the Nazi era and survived its aftermath. He passed away on April 13, 2015, in Lübeck, Germany.His extraordinary first novel, Die Blechtrommel (The Tin Drum, 1959), brought him international acclaim and established him as a leading voice in Germany’s cultural and political discourse, with his writing often confronting uncomfortable truths about history, identity, and morality. In recognition of his profound impact on literature, Grass was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1999.His career spanned decades, marked by bold explorations of human flaws, societal contradictions, and the complexities of truth. He was also politically active, using his voice to challenge authority and provoke reflection.Quote of the Day by Günter Grass: Among his many thought‑provoking reflections, Grass once said, “No idea stays pure. Even the flowering of art isn't pure. And the sun has spots. All geniuses menstruate. On sorrow floats laughter. In the heart of roaring lurks silence. In angles lean compasses. But the circle, the circle is pure” Günter Grass Quote: Context, meaning and interpretationThe quote reflects Grass’ worldview that perfection is elusive in human life, art, and thought. He recognized that contradictions, flaws, and paradoxes are inherent in existence. Yet, he pointed to the circle as a symbol of purity, an ideal form untouched by the imperfections that define everything else.Günter’s words suggest that purity is rare and perhaps unattainable in human endeavors. Ideas evolve, art carries imperfections, and even brilliance is marked by vulnerability. Grass juxtaposes sorrow and laughter, noise and silence, angles and compasses, to show that life is full of contradictions. The circle, however, stands as a metaphor for completeness and harmony, representing the unattainable ideal.His quote reminds us that imperfection is natural and should be embraced rather than denied. Dreams, art, and genius are all shaped by flaws, yet those flaws make them real and human. His reflection teaches us to accept contradictions, to find beauty in imperfection, and to strive for balance even when perfection is out of reach. The circle becomes a guiding symbol, an aspiration toward wholeness, even if life itself remains imperfect.
items.snippet: Nobel laureate Günter Grass, a pivotal post-war German writer, explored historical truths and human flaws in works like  The Tin Drum.  His quote  But the circle, the circle is pure  symbolizes an elusive ideal of perfection amidst life's inherent contradictions and imperfections. Grass's legacy lies in confronting uncomfortable realities and embracing the human condition.

items.headline: MC Interview: India has AI talent but lacks breakout ideas, says Y Combinator's Jared Friedman
items.body: Jared Friedman, Partner and Managing Director, Y Combinator As Jared Friedman prepares to host Y Combinator’s first-ever Startup School India at a massive hall in Bengaluru, his message is clear: India has the talent, but it needs bolder ideas-especially in AI. YC, the Silicon Valley accelerator behind global giants like Airbnb, Stripe and OpenAI, has backed several Indian startups so far. It has invested hundreds of millions of dollars and has generated outsized returns from bets on companies such as Razorpay, Meesho, Groww and Zepto and stands to gain more as they head toward a public market listing. Friedman, who co-founded Scribd-one of YC’s early success stories, now leads software investments at YC as Managing Director and General Partner. In an interview with Moneycontrol on the sidelines of Emergent Vibecon 2026, Friedman also spoke about India’s “second wave” of startups building for global markets, the criticism around the accelerator forcing Indian companies to domicile to the US and why it’s challenging for US based investors to fund Indian entities. EDITED EXCERPTS: Related Stories Y Combinator to back Indian founders building for global markets in second wave: Jared Friedman Former Oura CEO Harpreet Singh Rai joins Loop Health to lead healthcare business You’re bringing Y Combinator's Startup School to India for the very first time. What is your view on the India market? We're very bullish on India, that's why we're doing Startup School in India for the first time. We will have 2,500 people who are going to show up for the first Startup School India. If one looks at YC's portfolio here, you've had some very good outcomes, whether it's Razorpay, Meesho, Groww, Zepto. You placed more bets on the consumer side in the first wave and Indian companies building for India. How is the next wave going to be different? We have been investing in Indian companies for about 10 years, since 2015, when we funded Razorpay. And we've gotten to see some of the founders that we invested in back when they were often just recent grads from school, go on to build these epic companies that are now world famous. And we're coming all the way to India, because we see that there is an opportunity now for a second wave of Indian companies. The first wave was, like you said, companies building Indian products for the Indian market. I'm sure that that will continue. But now we're seeing a second wave of companies from India, which is companies building global products for the global market. And at Startup School India, we have two great examples of that - Emergent and Giga. They were both from here, but Emergent and Giga are not products for the Indian market. Their customers are primarily in the US and abroad. And one of the reasons that we wanted to come to India was to inspire more of the talented builders here to build those kinds of products. While YC has played a very important role in nurturing the ecosystem here, one criticism is that you force companies to flip to the US, and a lot of them have had to pay billions of dollars in taxes to flip back to India, as they look at listing here. Has that made you rethink on what you want the newer companies to do? It's very unfortunate. We wish that we could just fund Indian companies. We would love to do that. But the Indian government makes it very challenging for US based investors to fund Indian entities. It's not only a problem for us, but also a problem for all the US-based investors that would follow Y Combinator and invest in the companies after us. I wish I had a solution to this problem. But what I can say is that in the meantime, the fact that more and more of the companies coming from India are building for the global market suggests to me that that might be at least a partial solution, which is that if you're building a company like Emergent or Giga, actually the headquarters are in the US, even if a lot of the headcount is in India, and the customers are all in the US and the investors are mostly in the US, maybe it makes more sense for you to be a US entity. And the fact that we can't fund Indian entities is less of a problem than it was in the past. But what if they want to go public in India, which is what we saw with Groww, Meesho and now Zepto and Razorpay… Well, that's what you saw with those companies, because those companies are really building for the Indian market. When Emergent and Giga go public, I don't think they're going to go public on the Indian market. I think they're going to go public in the US stock market. And a lot of Indian employees are going to make a lot of money. Huge win. What do you make of the AI scene in India? Are you seeing those levels of energy that one sees in the US here? That's another one of the reasons we wanted to come to India. It's because this moment is really the greatest moment in history to start a company. It's the greatest revolution in the field of computer science since the invention of the computer. And everyone in Silicon Valley is just obsessed and can't turn their eyes away from what is happening with AI, because it's probably the most important thing that will happen in any of our lifetimes. And we wanted to bring some of that energy that we experience every day in Silicon Valley here to Bangalore. And we're hoping to infect more of the young builders in India and get them just as excited and just as hyped about AI. And for India, do you see more opportunity in the application layer? Will you fund India-based frontier labs? We would happily fund India-based Frontier Labs. But if you look at Y Combinator's companies across the board, most of the companies are at the application layer. And that's the most obvious opportunity to go after from here. Double clicking on what you said earlier, that in the next wave, you will look at companies in India that will build for the world. From what you've seen and heard so far, what opportunities do you see? What’s so exciting about India is that the depth and the breadth of the engineering talent here is unparalleled. So, when a team here gets product market fit, they can scale up very rapidly and hire the best engineers in the world. And that is a huge advantage in a competitive market. There is a common meme on the internet that AI is overhyped and it's a bubble and it's going to pop. And from the students who I talk to, it seems like there are a lot of young people here who believe that. And I think that's unfortunate. Because I think that the people who will really succeed in this new era that we are in are the people who are optimistic about AI. You’ve spoken about the things that excite you, but we want to know some things about the Indian startup ecosystem that have not worked well for you, something that has disappointed you? I think we are not seeing as many great AI companies coming out of India as we think there should be given how much talent there is in the country. Why do you think that is? Not enough capital? I don't think it's a question of capital. I think it's a question of ideas. People have to be inspired to work on the right ideas. People have to believe that this is going to bring about a great future to want to work on. It’s a question of not enough people really believing that AI is going to create enormous opportunities and wanting to spend all their time learning about the latest AI tools and technologies and building with that. How do you keep up with AI? Twitter (X). Twitter and social media, which is great because you don't have to be in San Francisco to have access to that. Everyone everywhere in the world can read the same Twitter posts, follow the same YouTubers, see the same content that I see at Y Combinator two blocks from OpenAI at the center of the AI revolution. And that's why I feel so confident that the builders here, once they tune in, once they really start paying attention and they really start playing with this stuff, they're going to realize just how incredible it is and they're going to be inspired to go and build the next Emergent or the next Giga.
items.snippet: Indian government makes it very challenging for US-based investors to fund Indian entities. It's a problem for all the US-based investors, Friedman told Moneycontrol, explaining why Y Combinator asks startups to be headquartered in the US.

items.headline: The coolest ideas are often the oldest
items.body: When my father retired from diplomatic service in the mid-1980s, among the items he brought back to install at home was a 2 ton airconditioner. It fitted neatly in the space under the bedroom window. Only, the low-quality wiring of my parents' standard DDA 'self-financing' flat could not take the load of the foreign AC and the whole electrical system would blow out the moment they turned it on. So it remained decorative and they made do perfectly well with aircoolers.Gigantic aluminium aircoolers, usually assembled by local vendors on site using large fans and wood-shaving pads wetted by an internal watering systems were a ubiquitous feature of north Indian homes till the 1990s. The hum of those fans could be heard even if the units were placed outside. Today, ranks of split ACs are a common sight in urban homes instead, with the swankier ones investing in central airconditioning. Air coolers have moved far down the social ladder.When my mother was growing up in the scorching heat of north India in the 1940s, neither appliance was available; instead there were khus 'tatties' or screens on the verandahs which would be doused with water so that the hot, dry 'loo' winds would be cooled and scented with vetiver before they wafted into the bungalows. The advent of ceiling fans around that time also helped the cool air circulate. Once the monsoon arrived, those screens were no longer needed. Bungalows are now an endangered species around India and verandahs are no longer a popular architectural feature. Most Indian today would not have even heard of khus tatties either; besides, with water scarce even in the metros, who would want to 'waste' it on wetting screens? Ceiling fans and air conditioners bought on monthly instalments are the easiest options, and family outings to AC shopping malls and leisure centres are the preferred peak summer activities.Yet even now, only 10% of Indian homes have airconditioning (that percentage doubles if aircoolers are included), skewed heavily in favour of urban areas, obviously. While analysts using western "models" conclude that there are "thousands of excessive deaths" every summer due to heat, it is not substantiated even by anecdotal evidence. Which implies that most Indians still weather our scorching summers like our ancestors did, by seeking other ways to stay cool.Primarily that means sticking to traditional architecture, clothing and diets that mitigate heat. Our buildings used to be made with cool materials, designed for cross-ventilation and orientated to avoid direct sunlight in summer. Our clothes were traditionally unstitched and light coloured, allowed for airflow to cool the body and protected the skin against the sun too. And our summer diets were light on spice, full of water-heavy vegetables, natural probiotics and electrolytes.Unfortunately, "progress" and globalisation have meant the jettisoning of many of these terroir-specific features by Indian city dwellers. Our urban planners, architects and builders do not care about making buildings that suit local climates, our current clothing norms also ignore the weather. And diets now hardly change according to the seasons, with spices, oil and preservative-laden convenience foods dominating our peripatetic lives. Yet we "worry" about global warming!None of these "globalised" norms can be changed in a hurry, of course. It has to be preceded by us Indians getting over our fascination for foreign prescriptions and fashions peddled under the specious excuse of modernity. Only when we come to terms with the exigencies of where we are, can we begin to think about what can be changed, and even what we can actually do without - sometimes willy-nilly as in the case of my late parents and their unusable foreign AC.
items.snippet: We need to think about what can be changed and what we can do without

items.headline: Delimitation row: Amit Shah says opposition not only against the bill, but the very idea of 'women's reservation'
items.body: Amit Shah (file image) Addressing the Lok Sabha on the three bills introduced by the Centre, Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday said that the opposition is not only opposing the three bills, but they are opposing the very idea of 'women's reservation." Those who are opposing delimitation are also opposing election of more SC/ST leaders, Shah added saying the Modi government had decided to go ahead with the bills to empower women and give them a political voice in India's democratic polity. "Every MP from the INDIA alliance has tried to oppose women's reservation," said Shah. "No one has objected to the women's reservation. But, if we see closely, all members of the INDI alliance have opposed it by using 'ifs and but' ", Shah added, replying to the debate on the Women's Reservation Bill and the Delimitation Bill in the Lok Sabha The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to tweak the women's quota law was introduced in Lok Sabha on Thursday after a division of votes. Two ordinary bills -- the Delimitation Bill and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill to implement the proposed amended women's quota law in Union territories of Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir -- were also introduced in the House. Related Stories Monsoon Session LIVE: Rajya Sabha passes Tribunal Reforms Bill 2026; both Houses adjourned for the d... Amit Shah to speak on students' protest in Parliament; Rahul Gandhi says 'not interested in fantasy ... Amit Shah ready to discuss Delhi Police action on CJP protesters in Parliament, says Kiren Rijiju The Home Minister added that the objective of all three bills is women’s empowerment, questioning how a single MP can represent nearly 49 lakh voters in one constituency. He accused the opposition of opposing the content of the women’s reservation bill rather than its procedure, adding that around 130 MPs spoke on the bill, including 56 women MPs. Earlier today, in a friendly banter, Leader of Opposition (LoP) in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Friday said that Prime Minister Narendra Modi and he didn't have "the wife issue", as the Congress MP emphasised that everyone has learnt from women in their lives. Participating in a debate in the Lok Sabha on the three bills introduced to amend the women's quota law and to set up a delimitation commission, Gandhi said women are a driving force in the national imagination and perspective.
items.snippet: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to tweak the women's quota law was introduced in Lok Sabha on Thursday after a division of votes.

items.headline: Vodafone Idea counters Airtel’s priority plan with everyone matters campaign
items.body: Vodafone Idea launched a campaign assuring its entire user base of postpaid and prepaid of receiving equal priority or treatment amidst Bharti Airtel rolling out its Priority Postpaid plan which provides a more stable telecom experience to its premium postpaid users. The third-largest telecom operator has openly taken a stance opposing the move by its rival, promising to treat all its users with equal priority.Also Read: Telecom industry divided on Airtel's 5G priority plan; Jio, Vi call for regulatory clarity “India’s digital growth has been built on the foundation of affordable and connectivity for all. At Vi, we strongly believe that every customer deserves a fair and consistent network experience. Offering preferential speeds or services based on user profile, raises questions around equity and principles of an equal digital ecosystem,” Avneesh Khosla, CMO, Vodafone Idea said in a statement.He added that for India to continue its digital growth, even as the technology advances, it is important for innovation and monetisation models to keep the interests of all customers paramount, be transparent and most of all remain inclusive.“Everyone is a priority with Vi. That’s why we’re continuously strengthening our network – We have added 2,20,000+ new towers, expanding Vi 5G in 110+ cities, and AI-based self-optimising network technology that intelligently adapts to help deliver stronger connectivity – even in crowded areas,” Vi said in a post on X, adding that a stronger network should feel strong for everyone, everywhere. The company’s shares hit a 52-week high of Rs 14.29 on Wednesday. Since Airtel launched its priority plan utilizing 5G network slicing, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) as well as Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) have been examining the service for violations of net neutrality norms and non-discriminatory access to mobile consumers. Vi has said such priority plans should be put on hold till there is clarity. Country’s largest operator Reliance Jio has also said such plans should be rolled out only after proper consultation with the government.Even as the authorities discuss the regulatory metrics, competition has been intensifying among the telcos to retain their premium subscribers from shifting to Airtel in a bid to get better services. In response to Airtel’s priority postpaid plans, Reliance Jio also announced an aggressive prepaid plan on Wednesday bundling over 15 premium Over-The-Top (OTT) subscriptions and 1000+ live TV channels along with 30GB 4G data and unlimited 5G access for 28 days. The plan is priced aggressively at Rs 200.
items.snippet: Vodafone Idea has launched a campaign promising equal network priority for all its users, directly opposing Bharti Airtel's new Priority Postpaid plan. Vi's CMO stated that preferential treatment raises questions about equity in the digital ecosystem. The company is investing in network expansion and AI technology to ensure consistent connectivity for everyone.

items.headline: Trump says he has 'no idea' how talks will go with Iran
items.body: Donald Trump (file photo) US President Donald Trump confirmed in a phone interview with NewsNation that talks among the US, Iran and Pakistan had begun, though he does not know how successful they could be. When asked how negotiations would go, Trump said: “I have no idea.” The US president said he would know shortly if he felt Iran was acting in good faith about resolving the war. Trump added that the US knew where mines had been placed in the Strait of Hormuz and that the military was bringing equipment to remove them.
items.snippet: When asked how negotiations would go, Trump said: “I have no idea.”

items.headline: 'Foolish idea': Congress slams Maharashtra govt's move to make Marathi mandatory for auto drivers
items.body: Transport Minister Sarnaik warned that action will be taken against those who do not follow the rules after checking by May 1 Congress MLA Nana Patole on Saturday slammed the state government's move to make Marathi mandatory for auto taxi drivers in Maharashtra, labelling the move as "nothing but a foolish idea" and an attempt to break Maharashtra and destroy its heritage. Speaking to ANI, Nana Patole warned that the Maharashtra government is bringing its own downfall by imposing Marathi on people. "The government seems intent on bringing about its own downfall. We are Indians, and our nation's identity lies in its diversity of languages, religions, and castes... To attempt to break Maharashtra based on language and destroy its heritage is nothing but a foolish idea," said Patole. Earlier, Samajwadi Party (SP) leader Abu Asim Azmi also opposed the move, saying every state has its own language and it's not fair to pressure students. While speaking to ANI on the issue, Azmi said, "Every state has its own language. If it's to be made compulsory, schools should teach Marathi first, especially for those who aren't proficient. Every country has its own language, so where will Hindi, the national language, be spoken?" Related Stories Bengaluru second airport: Congress tussle widens as Karnataka deputy CM proposes Tumakuru, CM DK Shi... BJP calls Rahul Gandhi 'prince with a disturbed mind', slams Congress leader for Parliament logjam Maharashtra plans EV charging stations at RTOs, MSRTC depots and flyovers across state "If you want people to learn Marathi, provide books and classes, don't pressure them," he added. These reactions come after the State Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik announced that the Marathi language will be made mandatory for driving rickshaws in the state. Speaking at a press conference, Sarnaik said that the decision applies to all rickshaw drivers in the state, not just Mira Bhayandar, as earlier reported. Transport Minister Sarnaik warned that action will be taken against those who do not follow the rules after checking by May 1. Drivers will be required to show they can read, write, and speak Marathi as part of the new initiative. This pilot project aims to tackle irregularities in issuing transport licences and will be rolled out statewide over time.
items.snippet: Congress leader Nana Patole warned that the Maharashtra government is bringing its own downfall by imposing Marathi on people.

items.headline: Employee on paid leave receives surprise job call. His next idea turned it into a promotion and big salary
items.body: In many workplaces, salary discussions and promotions tend to move slowly until something forces a decision. In a recent Reddit post an employee described how a normal break from work ended up triggering a job offer, a resignation plan, and eventually a large pay increase from his current employer after a sudden counteroffer situation unfolded.A Reddit user recently shared an experience that started off like any normal paid time off but quickly turned into something he did not expect. He explained that he had mixed feelings about his current workplace, saying, “I like the company I work for, I don’t love it. I’ve learned a lot here but I’d leave for the right role somewhere else. Also they have a gym onsite which is a big plus.”At the same time, he also mentioned he wasn’t actively job hunting in a serious way because the company had recently been acquired and there were financial benefits tied to staying on.The unexpected call during leaveThings changed when he was on PTO and received a call from a local company. According to him, the recruiter said they were “desperate to fill a role you’d be perfect for.” He initially pushed the interview to the following week, but the company insisted on moving fast and arranged an online interview the same day with the full team.The interview went unusually quickly. He was given a job offer almost immediately, and the formal offer letter arrived the next morning.Reflecting on the situation, he wrote, “I was soft looking but nothing serious because the company was just bought out by one of the biggest companies in the world.” He also explained that he had retention bonuses and payouts lined up over the next couple of years, which made leaving a complicated decision.Even so, the new offer changed the situation enough for him to take action at his current workplace.Returning to work with an offer in handAfter returning from leave, he submitted his resignation. The reaction from his manager was immediate and emotional. He recalled her saying, “oh god, please, no. Please be joking.”The matter escalated quickly to senior leadership. The CEO, who was the former owner before the acquisition, directly intervened. The employee said the CEO told him, “don’t BS me, show me the offer letter and I’ll beat it by $5,000 today.”After reviewing the external offer, the company responded the same day. The employee received a 35% pay increase, a promotion to Senior Manager, and a written commitment for a Director-level promotion within a year.He later summed up the experience simply: “Best PTO I’ve ever had.”Mixed reactions and workplace realityThe post also sparked discussion among other users. Some pointed out that companies often react strongly only when an employee is about to leave, with one comment saying that notice tends to unlock budgets that were previously unavailable.Others shared similar stories of receiving large raises only after resigning or being rehired later at higher pay. A few users also warned that counteroffers don’t always guarantee long-term stability, arguing that the underlying reasons for leaving can still remain.The employee himself suggested the outcome was a mix of timing, company transitions, and his own position in the organization. While he accepted the counteroffer and improved role, he also acknowledged the uncertainty that often comes with such decisions.
items.snippet: A Reddit user shared how a routine paid time off unexpectedly turned into a major career moment after he received a sudden job offer during his leave. Although he was not actively job hunting, the fast-moving interview process led to an immediate offer, prompting him to resign from his current role. However, instead of losing him, his employer quickly responded with a counteroffer, matching and exceeding the opportunity.

items.headline: Going all-in on one investment idea. Why it usually backfires
items.body: Representative image Concentrating on one investment heightens risk and stress Diversification cuts concentration risk, stabilizing results Timing matters more when your portfolio is tied to a single idea Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan There’s always that one idea that feels right. A stock everyone is talking about. A sector that seems unstoppable. A fund that has been performing well for a while. At some point, it stops feeling like a choice and starts feeling like the obvious thing to do. That’s usually when people go all-in. It feels efficient. Instead of spreading your money around, you’re backing something you understand and believe in. If it works, the gains feel more meaningful. There’s no dilution, no second-guessing. But what gets missed in that moment is how much depends on that one decision. When one idea becomes your entire outcome Related Stories Quote of the day by Chris Rock: "Wealth is not about having a lot of money; it's about having a lot ... Axis Pension Fund CEO bats for EPF-NPS merger, says reform 'waiting to happen' Planning a short international trip? Here's how to get more value from your travel budget The problem with going all-in isn’t just risk in the usual sense. It’s concentration. When all your money is tied to one idea, your entire outcome depends on how that one thing plays out. If it works, everything looks great. If it doesn’t, there’s nothing balancing it out. And markets don’t move in straight lines. Even strong ideas go through phases where they stall, correct or underperform for long stretches. That’s often when doubt starts creeping in. Timing matters more than you think Even a good investment can feel like a bad one if you enter at the wrong time. When you go all-in, timing becomes more important than it should be. There’s no room to average out or adjust gradually. You’re exposed to whatever happens next. If the market turns soon after you invest, the losses feel sharper because you don’t have anything else holding up your portfolio. It becomes harder to stay rational When one idea dominates your portfolio, it also starts to dominate your thinking. Every price movement feels personal. You check it more often. You react more quickly. Small changes start to feel bigger than they are. That emotional pressure can lead to decisions you wouldn’t otherwise make. Holding on too long, or exiting too early, both become more likely. What feels like conviction can actually be risk There’s a fine line between confidence and overexposure. Believing in an idea is not the issue. The issue is how much of your portfolio depends on it. When everything is tied to one outcome, even a small shift in that idea can have a disproportionate impact on your finances. Why spreading out usually works better Diversification isn’t about playing it safe. It’s about not letting one decision define everything. When your money is spread across different assets or ideas, the pressure on each one reduces. Some will do well, some won’t, but the overall impact becomes more stable. It also gives you the ability to adjust over time instead of being locked into one position. What this really comes down to Going all-in feels simple and decisive. It gives you a clear bet and a clear outcome. But investing rarely works that cleanly. What looks like a strong idea today can take longer than expected, move differently than expected or simply not play out the way you imagined. And when everything is riding on that one idea, the downside becomes much harder to manage than it seemed at the start.
items.snippet: It feels confident and decisive in the moment, but putting all your money in one place often creates risks you don’t see immediately.

items.headline: Only one person in inner circle opposed Iran war, told Trump it's a 'bad idea’: Inside story
items.body: As the dust settles on the 40-day Iran war and a fragile ceasefire takes hold, details are emerging about how the conflict started and what drove US President Donald Trump, who describes himself as a man of peace, to launch one of the deadliest conflicts in West Asia in recent years. A New York Times report, citing a forthcoming book “Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump " by journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, said that Israel PM Benjamin Netanyahu made a detailed pitch to Trump and his team in the White House Situation Room at one of the meetings before the war. The report said that Netanyahu, during an hour-long presentation, said that it was the right time to launch an attack on Iran, which was "ripe for a regime change". He outlined a scenario in which an attack would deliver a “near-certain victory,” with Iran’s nuclear programme dismantled within weeks and the Strait of Hormuz kept open. He also suggested that Mossad could help foment internal unrest in Iran to finish the job. Notably, US intelligence officials said that a regime change in Iran would be "farcical" but agreed to the possibility of killing the Ayatollah and crippling the country's ability to threaten its neighbors, the report said. The Outlier Notably, while most of Trump's advisors refrained from counselling him against an attack, only one dissenting emerged: that of Vice President JD Vance. The report claimed that Vance was the strongest opponent of the war and even made a forceful case against it. According to the NYT report, Vance, who had opposed military adventurism throughout his political career, told Trump's inner circle that a war with Iran to change its regime "would be a disaster". Vance made a strong case in front of Trump himself and warned of "untold casualties" and "regional chaos" in the event of a war, the report said. He also argued that a conflict could be seen as a "betrayal" by voters who supported Trump on the promise of "no new wars". He also warned of the depletion of US ammunitions and the risk of an "outsized and unpredictable retaliation", which later played out exactly how he predicted. Vance also warned about the Strait of Hormuz and the likelihood of soaring gasoline prices, the report said. "His preference was for no strikes at all. But knowing Trump was likely to act, Vance tried to steer him toward more limited options," the report said. In his final meeting before the attack, Vance ultimately accepted the decision, telling Donald Trump: “ You know I think this is a bad idea, but if you want to do it, I’ll support you .” The report said that while privately, people in Trump's inner circle took different positions on the war, nobody except Vance put forth a "forceful argument" to change Trump’s mind.

items.headline: Rs 1 lakh salary, but daily office stress ruined her life: One idea later, she doubled her income and redu
items.body: For many people, earning around Rs 1 lakh every month is seen as a stable and successful life. But for one young professional, the reality behind that salary looked very different. The long hours, constant stress, and pressure from work had slowly started affecting her daily life to the point where she no longer felt happy doing what she once worked hard for.Content creator Mehar Verma recently spoke about her career shift in an Instagram post where she explained why she decided to leave her law career behind, despite having what many would consider a secure and well-paying job.According to her post, she was working at a law firm in February 2024 and earning nearly Rs 1 lakh a month. Still, she said she felt miserable most of the time.“In Feb 2024, I was working at a law firm, earning around ₹1 lakh a month. On paper, everything looked sorted. But I was miserable,” she wrote.Long work hours and stress pushed her toward burnoutShe explained that her routine had become exhausting. Most days involved long hours at work, little personal time, and carrying work pressure back home even late at night.“Long hours, no real weekends, coming home at 9–10 PM and still working. I was constantly tired, constantly stressed, and honestly I dreaded most days,” she shared.Over time, she realised the problem was not temporary stress but a deeper feeling that the profession itself no longer felt right for her. She said there was no dramatic turning point behind her decision, only a quiet feeling that she did not want this life anymore.“At some point, I realised I didn’t want to be a lawyer. There was no big moment, just a quiet, persistent feeling that this wasn’t the life I wanted,” she said.Eventually, she decided to leave her job even though she did not have another career fully planned out. “So I quit. No solid plan. No backup.”131314298The transition period was difficultLeaving a stable profession did not instantly improve things for her. In the same post, she admitted that the months after quitting were emotionally difficult and financially uncertain.“And it wasn’t easy.
